# walkdir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/walkdir/

## Expand description

Crate `walkdir` provides an efficient and cross platform implementation
of recursive directory traversal. Several options are exposed to control
iteration, such as whether to follow symbolic links (default off), limit the
maximum number of simultaneous open file descriptors and the ability to
efficiently skip descending into directories.

To use this crate, add `walkdir` as a dependency to your project’s
`Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
walkdir = "2"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#from-the-top)From the top

The [ WalkDir](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html) type builds iterators. The

[type describes values yielded by the iterator. Finally, the](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html)

`DirEntry`[type is a small wrapper around](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)

`Error`[with additional information, such as if a loop was detected while following symbolic links (not enabled by default).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/struct.Error.html)

`std::io::Error`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following code recursively iterates over the directory given and prints the path for each entry:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo") {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
Or, if you’d like to iterate over all entries and ignore any errors that
may arise, use [ filter_map](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.filter_map). (e.g., This code below will silently skip
directories that the owner of the running process does not have permission to
access.)

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter().filter_map(|e| e.ok()) {
    println!("{}", entry.path().display());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-follow-symbolic-links)Example: follow symbolic links

The same code as above, except [ follow_links](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.follow_links) is enabled:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").follow_links(true) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-skip-hidden-files-and-directories-on-unix)Example: skip hidden files and directories on unix

This uses the [ filter_entry](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html#method.filter_entry) iterator adapter to avoid yielding hidden files
and directories efficiently (i.e. without recursing into hidden directories):

```
use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
    entry.file_name()
         .to_str()
         .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
         .unwrap_or(false)
}
let walker = WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter();
for entry in walker.filter_entry(|e| !is_hidden(e)) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DirEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html)
- A directory entry.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error produced by recursively walking a directory.
- [Filter](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterEntry.html)- Entry
- A recursive directory iterator that skips entries.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator for recursively descending into a directory.
- [WalkDir](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html)
- A builder to create an iterator for recursively walking a directory.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [DirEntry](https://docs.rs/trait.DirEntryExt.html)- Ext
- Unix-specific extension methods for `walkdir::DirEntry`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A result type for walkdir operations.

# same_file - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/same-file/^1.0.1/

## Expand description

This crate provides a safe and simple **cross platform** way to determine
whether two file paths refer to the same file or directory.

Most uses of this crate should be limited to the top-level [ is_same_file](https://docs.rs/fn.is_same_file.html)
function, which takes two file paths and returns true if they refer to the
same file or directory:

```
use same_file::is_same_file;
assert!(is_same_file("/bin/sh", "/usr/bin/sh")?);
```
Additionally, this crate provides a [ Handle](https://docs.rs/struct.Handle.html) type that permits a more efficient
equality check depending on your access pattern. For example, if one wanted to
check whether any path in a list of paths corresponded to the process’ stdout
handle, then one could build a handle once for stdout. The equality check for
each file in the list then only requires one stat call instead of two. The code
might look like this:

```
use same_file::Handle;
let candidates = &[
    "examples/is_same_file.rs",
    "examples/is_stderr.rs",
    "examples/stderr",
];
let stdout_handle = Handle::stdout()?;
for candidate in candidates {
    let handle = Handle::from_path(candidate)?;
    if stdout_handle == handle {
        println!("{:?} is stdout!", candidate);
    } else {
        println!("{:?} is NOT stdout!", candidate);
    }
}
```
See [ examples/is_stderr.rs](https://github.com/BurntSushi/same-file/blob/master/examples/is_same_file.rs) for a runnable example and compare the output of:

- `cargo run --example is_stderr 2> examples/stderr`and
- `cargo run --example is_stderr`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Handle](https://docs.rs/struct.Handle.html)
- A handle to a file that can be tested for equality with other handles.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_same_file.html)- same_ - file
- Returns true if the two file paths may correspond to the same file.

# doc_comment - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/doc-comment/^0.3/

## Expand description

The point of this (small) crate is to allow you to add doc comments from macros or
to test external markdown files’ code blocks through `rustdoc`.

Starting in Rust 1.54, this crate becomes useless as you can do the same thing
with the `doc` attribute:

[§](https://docs.rs#including-files-for-testing)Including file(s) for testing

Let’s assume you want to test code examples in your `README.md` file which
looks like this:

```
# A crate
Here is a code example:
```rust
let x = 2;
assert!(x != 0);
```
```
You can use the `doc_comment!` macro to test it like this:

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate doc_comment;
// When running `cargo test`, rustdoc will check this file as well.
doc_comment!(include_str!("../README.md"));
```
Please note that can also use the `doctest!` macro to have a shorter way to test an outer
file:

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate doc_comment;
doctest!("../README.md");
```
Please also note that you can use `#[cfg(doctest)]`:

```
#[cfg(doctest)]
doctest!("../README.md");
```
In this case, the examples in the `README.md` file will only be run on `cargo test`. You
can find more information about `#[cfg(doctest)]` in [this blogpost](https://blog.guillaume-gomez.fr/articles/2020-03-07+cfg%28doctest%29+is+stable+and+you+should+use+it).

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-documentation)Generic documentation

Now let’s imagine you want to write documentation once for multiple types but still having examples specific to each type:

```
// The macro which generates types
macro_rules! gen_types {
    ($tyname:ident) => {
        /// This is a wonderful generated struct!
        ///
        /// You can use it as follow:
        ///
        /// ```
        /// let x = FirstOne {
        ///     field1: 0,
        ///     field2: 0,
        ///     field3: 0,
        ///     field4: 0,
        /// };
        ///
        /// println!("Created a new instance of FirstOne: {:?}", x);
        /// ```
        #[derive(Debug)]
        pub struct $tyname {
            pub field1: u8,
            pub field2: u16,
            pub field3: u32,
            pub field4: u64,
        }
    }
}
// Now let's actually generate types:
gen_types!(FirstOne);
gen_types!(SecondOne);
gen_types!(Another);
```
So now we have created three structs with different names, but they all have the exact same
documentation, which is an issue for any structs not called `FirstOne`. That’s where
[ doc_comment!](https://docs.rs/macro.doc_comment.html) macro comes in handy!

Let’s rewrite the `gen_types!` macro:

```
// Of course, we need to import the `doc_comment` macro:
#[macro_use]
extern crate doc_comment;
macro_rules! gen_types {
    ($tyname:ident) => {
        doc_comment! {
concat!("This is a wonderful generated struct!
You can use it as follow:
```
let x = ", stringify!($tyname), " {
    field1: 0,
    field2: 0,
    field3: 0,
    field4: 0,
};
println!(\"Created a new instance of ", stringify!($tyname), ": {:?}\", x);
```"),
            #[derive(Debug)]
            pub struct $tyname {
                pub field1: u8,
                pub field2: u16,
                pub field3: u32,
                pub field4: u64,
            }
        }
    }
}
gen_types!(FirstOne);
gen_types!(SecondOne);
gen_types!(Another);
```
Now each struct has doc which match itself!

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [doc_](https://docs.rs/macro.doc_comment.html)- comment
- This macro can be used to generate documentation upon a type/item (or just to test outer markdown file code examples).
- [doctest](https://docs.rs/macro.doctest.html)
- This macro provides a simpler way to test an outer markdown file.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# scryone - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/scryone/0.2.0/scryone/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scryone)Scryone

Crate for providing an API Client, Types, and Request objects for working with the [Scryfall
API](https://scryfall.com/docs/api)

It offers the following:

- Types to represent Scryfall Objects (e.g. Cards, Sets, Rulings etc).
- Asynchronous and blocking API Clients to communicate with Scryfall
- Request types and builders for building requests to each of Scryfall API’s endpoints

[§](https://docs.rs#requests)Requests

Scryfall has many endpoints for different aspects of their API.
To help you execute queries against certain endpoints, `scryone` provides
[ Request](https://docs.rs/api/request/index.html) types and
builders for them which allow you to set all parameters that Scryfall allows.

Each Request type implements a trait called [ ScryfallRequest](https://docs.rs/api/request/trait.ScryfallRequest.html) which automatically builds the appropriate URL
for the API based on the parameters that you have set.

For example, creating a request to search for a specific card (`/cards/search` endpoint in
Scryfall):

```
let request = CardSearchRequest::builder()
    .query("Winter Orb")
    .unique_mode(UniqueMode::Cards)
    .sort_order(SortOrder::Set)
    .sort_direction(SortDirection::Desc)
    .data_format(DataFormat::Json)
    .build()?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#api-clients)API Clients

An [ asynchronous](https://docs.rs/api/struct.ScryfallClient.html) and

[client are supplied to enable you to contact Scryfall’s API.](https://docs.rs/api/blocking/struct.ScryfallClient.html)

`blocking`The clients offer the following:

-
GET requests to the endpoint that accepts a `ScryfallRequest`
-
POST requests to endpoints that allow it (only one single API endpoints supports this as of now).
-
Generic GET requests that allow you to define the type you wish to deserialize into (you must provide the URL)
-
Paginated requests that automatically (and respectfully) retrieve all data from paginated responses from Scryfall.

Example:

```
let client = ScryfallClient::new();
let request = CardSearchRequest::builder()
    .query("Winter Orb")
    .unique_mode(UniqueMode::Cards)
    .sort_order(SortOrder::Set)
    .sort_direction(SortDirection::Desc)
    .data_format(DataFormat::Json)
    .build()?;
// Automatically constructs the appropriate URL for the `/cards/search` endpoint
let response: List<Vec<Card>> = client.get(request).await?;
println!("Total cards: {:?}", response.total_cards);
println!("Cards: {:?}", response.data);
```

# sim_lib_discrete_comb - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-discrete-comb/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_discrete_comb/

## Expand description

Discrete combinatorics.

This crate hosts exact counting functions (over `num_bigint::BigUint`), lazy
enumerators, and canonical combinadic / Lehmer / mixed-radix rank-unrank
helpers. These ordinals are the bridge to rank, but this crate never depends
on `sim-lib-rank`.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use bit_vector::`- [BitVectorIter](https://docs.rs/bit_vector/struct.BitVectorIter.html);

# viterbi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/viterbi/0.0.1/viterbi/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#viterbi--ccsds-k7-r12-convolutional-encoder--hard-decision-block-viterbi-decoder)`viterbi` — CCSDS K=7 R=1/2 convolutional encoder + hard-decision block Viterbi decoder.

This crate is the **inner code** of the classic CCSDS concatenated coding scheme
(`K = 7`, `R = 1/2`), designed to pair with an outer Reed–Solomon code via an interleaver:

```
TX:  data → [RS(255,223)] → [interleaver] → [conv. K=7] → CHANNEL
RX:  CHANNEL → [Viterbi] → [de-interleaver] → [RS decode] → data
               └── this crate
```
This increment (`v0.0.x`) provides **hard-decision, block-mode** encode/decode targeting `std`.
Soft-decision, puncturing, rate 1/3, and generic `K ≤ 9` are additive in the next minor.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-invariants)Design invariants

- Pure Rust, no `unsafe`(`forbid`ed crate-wide via`Cargo.toml`lints and here).
- Deterministic: same input ⇒ same output, bit-for-bit, on every platform.
- No panic in the decode hot path; `Result`only at configuration boundaries.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Encode a payload, then recover it with the Viterbi decoder (clean channel):

```
use viterbi::{CcsdsViterbiDecoder, CodeParams, ViterbiEncoder};
// Build the encoder and decoder from the first-class CCSDS profile.
let encoder = ViterbiEncoder::new(CodeParams::ccsds_r1_2()).unwrap();
let mut decoder = CcsdsViterbiDecoder::new(CodeParams::ccsds_r1_2(), 4096).unwrap();
let payload = b"hello, viterbi";
let coded = encoder.encode(payload).unwrap();
let decoded = decoder.decode_block(&coded).unwrap();
assert_eq!(&decoded.bytes, payload);
```

# knok - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/knok/0.3.2/knok/

## Expand description

Static-shape tensor containers and runtime wrappers for build-time traced IREE VM bytecode artifacts.

Graphs are authored from `build.rs` with `knok-build`, which executes traced
Rust functions on the compile host and writes generated artifact wrappers to
`OUT_DIR`. Target crates import those wrappers with `generated_graphs!`:

For repeated hosted inference, construct one [ Engine](https://docs.rs/runtime/struct.Engine.html) and call generated

`graphs::<name>::run(&engine, ...)` wrappers.With default features disabled, `knok` is `no_std + alloc`; hosted runtime
execution is unavailable on the target unless the runtime feature set is
enabled.

# walkdir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/walkdir/2.5.0/target-redirect/walkdir/

## Expand description

Crate `walkdir` provides an efficient and cross platform implementation
of recursive directory traversal. Several options are exposed to control
iteration, such as whether to follow symbolic links (default off), limit the
maximum number of simultaneous open file descriptors and the ability to
efficiently skip descending into directories.

To use this crate, add `walkdir` as a dependency to your project’s
`Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
walkdir = "2"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#from-the-top)From the top

The [ WalkDir](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html) type builds iterators. The

[type describes values yielded by the iterator. Finally, the](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html)

`DirEntry`[type is a small wrapper around](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)

`Error`[with additional information, such as if a loop was detected while following symbolic links (not enabled by default).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/struct.Error.html)

`std::io::Error`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following code recursively iterates over the directory given and prints the path for each entry:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo") {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
Or, if you’d like to iterate over all entries and ignore any errors that
may arise, use [ filter_map](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.filter_map). (e.g., This code below will silently skip
directories that the owner of the running process does not have permission to
access.)

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter().filter_map(|e| e.ok()) {
    println!("{}", entry.path().display());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-follow-symbolic-links)Example: follow symbolic links

The same code as above, except [ follow_links](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.follow_links) is enabled:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").follow_links(true) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-skip-hidden-files-and-directories-on-unix)Example: skip hidden files and directories on unix

This uses the [ filter_entry](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html#method.filter_entry) iterator adapter to avoid yielding hidden files
and directories efficiently (i.e. without recursing into hidden directories):

```
use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
    entry.file_name()
         .to_str()
         .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
         .unwrap_or(false)
}
let walker = WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter();
for entry in walker.filter_entry(|e| !is_hidden(e)) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DirEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html)
- A directory entry.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error produced by recursively walking a directory.
- [Filter](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterEntry.html)- Entry
- A recursive directory iterator that skips entries.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator for recursively descending into a directory.
- [WalkDir](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html)

# walkdir/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)/*!
[2](https://docs.rs#2)Crate `walkdir` provides an efficient and cross platform implementation
[3](https://docs.rs#3)of recursive directory traversal. Several options are exposed to control
[4](https://docs.rs#4)iteration, such as whether to follow symbolic links (default off), limit the
[5](https://docs.rs#5)maximum number of simultaneous open file descriptors and the ability to
[6](https://docs.rs#6)efficiently skip descending into directories.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)
[8](https://docs.rs#8)To use this crate, add `walkdir` as a dependency to your project's
[9](https://docs.rs#9)`Cargo.toml`:
[10](https://docs.rs#10)
[11](https://docs.rs#11)```toml
[12](https://docs.rs#12)[dependencies]
[13](https://docs.rs#13)walkdir = "2"
[14](https://docs.rs#14)```
[15](https://docs.rs#15)
[16](https://docs.rs#16)# From the top
[17](https://docs.rs#17)
[18](https://docs.rs#18)The [`WalkDir`] type builds iterators. The [`DirEntry`] type describes values
[19](https://docs.rs#19)yielded by the iterator. Finally, the [`Error`] type is a small wrapper around
[20](https://docs.rs#20)[`std::io::Error`] with additional information, such as if a loop was detected
[21](https://docs.rs#21)while following symbolic links (not enabled by default).
[22](https://docs.rs#22)
[23](https://docs.rs#23)[`WalkDir`]: struct.WalkDir.html
[24](https://docs.rs#24)[`DirEntry`]: struct.DirEntry.html
[25](https://docs.rs#25)[`Error`]: struct.Error.html
[26](https://docs.rs#26)[`std::io::Error`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/struct.Error.html
[27](https://docs.rs#27)
[28](https://docs.rs#28)# Example
[29](https://docs.rs#29)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)The following code recursively iterates over the directory given and prints
[31](https://docs.rs#31)the path for each entry:
[32](https://docs.rs#32)
[33](https://docs.rs#33)```no_run
[34](https://docs.rs#34)use walkdir::WalkDir;
[35](https://docs.rs#35)# use walkdir::Error;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)
[37](https://docs.rs#37)# fn try_main() -> Result<(), Error> {
[38](https://docs.rs#38)for entry in WalkDir::new("foo") {
[39](https://docs.rs#39)    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
[40](https://docs.rs#40)}
[41](https://docs.rs#41)# Ok(())
[42](https://docs.rs#42)# }
[43](https://docs.rs#43)```
[44](https://docs.rs#44)
[45](https://docs.rs#45)Or, if you'd like to iterate over all entries and ignore any errors that
[46](https://docs.rs#46)may arise, use [`filter_map`]. (e.g., This code below will silently skip
[47](https://docs.rs#47)directories that the owner of the running process does not have permission to
[48](https://docs.rs#48)access.)
[49](https://docs.rs#49)
[50](https://docs.rs#50)```no_run
[51](https://docs.rs#51)use walkdir::WalkDir;
[52](https://docs.rs#52)
[53](https://docs.rs#53)for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter().filter_map(|e| e.ok()) {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)    println!("{}", entry.path().display());
[55](https://docs.rs#55)}
[56](https://docs.rs#56)```
[57](https://docs.rs#57)
[58](https://docs.rs#58)[`filter_map`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.filter_map
[59](https://docs.rs#59)
[60](https://docs.rs#60)# Example: follow symbolic links
[61](https://docs.rs#61)
[62](https://docs.rs#62)The same code as above, except [`follow_links`] is enabled:
[63](https://docs.rs#63)
[64](https://docs.rs#64)```no_run
[65](https://docs.rs#65)use walkdir::WalkDir;
[66](https://docs.rs#66)# use walkdir::Error;
[67](https://docs.rs#67)
[68](https://docs.rs#68)# fn try_main() -> Result<(), Error> {
[69](https://docs.rs#69)for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").follow_links(true) {
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
[71](https://docs.rs#71)}
[72](https://docs.rs#72)# Ok(())
[73](https://docs.rs#73)# }
[74](https://docs.rs#74)```
[75](https://docs.rs#75)
[76](https://docs.rs#76)[`follow_links`]: struct.WalkDir.html#method.follow_links
[77](https://docs.rs#77)
[78](https://docs.rs#78)# Example: skip hidden files and directories on unix
[79](https://docs.rs#79)
[80](https://docs.rs#80)This uses the [`filter_entry`] iterator adapter to avoid yielding hidden files
[81](https://docs.rs#81)and directories efficiently (i.e. without recursing into hidden directories):
[82](https://docs.rs#82)
[83](https://docs.rs#83)```no_run
[84](https://docs.rs#84)use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
[85](https://docs.rs#85)# use walkdir::Error;
[86](https://docs.rs#86)
[87](https://docs.rs#87)fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    entry.file_name()
[89](https://docs.rs#89)         .to_str()
[90](https://docs.rs#90)         .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
[91](https://docs.rs#91)         .unwrap_or(false)
[92](https://docs.rs#92)}
[93](https://docs.rs#93)
[94](https://docs.rs#94)# fn try_main() -> Result<(), Error> {
[95](https://docs.rs#95)let walker = WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter();
[96](https://docs.rs#96)for entry in walker.filter_entry(|e| !is_hidden(e)) {
[97](https://docs.rs#97)    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
[98](https://docs.rs#98)}
[99](https://docs.rs#99)# Ok(())
[100](https://docs.rs#100)# }
[101](https://docs.rs#101)```
[102](https://docs.rs#102)
[103](https://docs.rs#103)[`filter_entry`]: struct.IntoIter.html#method.filter_entry

[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// A result type for walkdir operations.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)///
[148](https://docs.rs#148)/// Note that this result type embeds the error type in this crate. This
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// is only useful if you care about the additional information provided by
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// the error (such as the path associated with the error or whether a loop
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// was dectected). If you want things to Just Work, then you can use
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// [`io::Result`] instead since the error type in this package will
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// automatically convert to an [`io::Result`] when using the [`try!`] macro.
[154](https://docs.rs#154)///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// [`io::Result`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/type.Result.html
[156](https://docs.rs#156)/// [`try!`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.try.html
[157](https://docs.rs#157)pub type Result<T> = ::std::result::Result<T, Error>;
[158](https://docs.rs#158)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)/// A builder to create an iterator for recursively walking a directory.
[160](https://docs.rs#160)///
[161](https://docs.rs#161)/// Results are returned in depth first fashion, with directories yielded
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// before their contents. If [`contents_first`] is true, contents are yielded
[163](https://docs.rs#163)/// before their directories. The order is unspecified but if [`sort_by`] is
[164](https://docs.rs#164)/// given, directory entries are sorted according to this function. Directory
[165](https://docs.rs#165)/// entries `.` and `..` are always omitted.
[166](https://docs.rs#166)///
[167](https://docs.rs#167)/// If an error occurs at any point during iteration, then it is returned in
[168](https://docs.rs#168)/// place of its corresponding directory entry and iteration continues as
[169](https://docs.rs#169)/// normal. If an error occurs while opening a directory for reading, then it
[170](https://docs.rs#170)/// is not descended into (but the error is still yielded by the iterator).
[171](https://docs.rs#171)/// Iteration may be stopped at any time. When the iterator is destroyed, all
[172](https://docs.rs#172)/// resources associated with it are freed.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)///
[174](https://docs.rs#174)/// [`contents_first`]: struct.WalkDir.html#method.contents_first
[175](https://docs.rs#175)/// [`sort_by`]: struct.WalkDir.html#method.sort_by
[176](https://docs.rs#176)///
[177](https://docs.rs#177)/// # Usage
[178](https://docs.rs#178)///
[179](https://docs.rs#179)/// This type implements [`IntoIterator`] so that it may be used as the subject
[180](https://docs.rs#180)/// of a `for` loop. You may need to call [`into_iter`] explicitly if you want
[181](https://docs.rs#181)/// to use iterator adapters such as [`filter_entry`].
[182](https://docs.rs#182)///
[183](https://docs.rs#183)/// Idiomatic use of this type should use method chaining to set desired
[184](https://docs.rs#184)/// options. For example, this only shows entries with a depth of `1`, `2` or
[185](https://docs.rs#185)/// `3` (relative to `foo`):
[186](https://docs.rs#186)///
[187](https://docs.rs#187)/// ```no_run
[188](https://docs.rs#188)/// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[189](https://docs.rs#189)/// # use walkdir::Error;
[190](https://docs.rs#190)///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)/// # fn try_main() -> Result<(), Error> {
[192](https://docs.rs#192)/// for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").min_depth(1).max_depth(3) {
[193](https://docs.rs#193)///     println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
[194](https://docs.rs#194)/// }
[195](https://docs.rs#195)/// # Ok(())
[196](https://docs.rs#196)/// # }
[197](https://docs.rs#197)/// ```
[198](https://docs.rs#198)///
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// [`IntoIterator`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/iter/trait.IntoIterator.html
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// [`into_iter`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/trait.IntoIterator.html#tymethod.into_iter
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// [`filter_entry`]: struct.IntoIter.html#method.filter_entry
[202](https://docs.rs#202)///
[203](https://docs.rs#203)/// Note that the iterator by default includes the top-most directory. Since
[204](https://docs.rs#204)/// this is the only directory yielded with depth `0`, it is easy to ignore it
[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// with the [`min_depth`] setting:
[206](https://docs.rs#206)///
[207](https://docs.rs#207)/// ```no_run
[208](https://docs.rs#208)/// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[209](https://docs.rs#209)/// # use walkdir::Error;
[210](https://docs.rs#210)///
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// # fn try_main() -> Result<(), Error> {
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").min_depth(1) {
[213](https://docs.rs#213)///     println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
[214](https://docs.rs#214)/// }
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// # Ok(())
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// # }
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// ```
[218](https://docs.rs#218)///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// [`min_depth`]: struct.WalkDir.html#method.min_depth
[220](https://docs.rs#220)///
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// This will only return descendents of the `foo` directory and not `foo`
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// itself.
[223](https://docs.rs#223)///
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// # Loops
[225](https://docs.rs#225)///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)/// This iterator (like most/all recursive directory iterators) assumes that
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// no loops can be made with *hard* links on your file system. In particular,
[228](https://docs.rs#228)/// this would require creating a hard link to a directory such that it creates
[229](https://docs.rs#229)/// a loop. On most platforms, this operation is illegal.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)///
[231](https://docs.rs#231)/// Note that when following symbolic/soft links, loops are detected and an
[232](https://docs.rs#232)/// error is reported.
[233](https://docs.rs#233)#[derive(Debug)]
[234](https://docs.rs#234)pub struct WalkDir {
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    opts: WalkDirOptions,
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    root: PathBuf,
[237](https://docs.rs#237)}
[238](https://docs.rs#238)

[280](https://docs.rs#280)
[281](https://docs.rs#281)impl WalkDir {
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// Create a builder for a recursive directory iterator starting at the
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    /// file path `root`. If `root` is a directory, then it is the first item
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// yielded by the iterator. If `root` is a file, then it is the first
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    /// and only item yielded by the iterator. If `root` is a symlink, then it
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// is always followed for the purposes of directory traversal. (A root
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    /// `DirEntry` still obeys its documentation with respect to symlinks and
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// the `follow_links` setting.)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    pub fn new<P: AsRef<Path>>(root: P) -> Self {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        WalkDir {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)            opts: WalkDirOptions {
[292](https://docs.rs#292)                follow_links: false,
[293](https://docs.rs#293)                follow_root_links: true,
[294](https://docs.rs#294)                max_open: 10,
[295](https://docs.rs#295)                min_depth: 0,
[296](https://docs.rs#296)                max_depth: ::std::usize::MAX,
[297](https://docs.rs#297)                sorter: None,
[298](https://docs.rs#298)                contents_first: false,
[299](https://docs.rs#299)                same_file_system: false,
[300](https://docs.rs#300)            },
[301](https://docs.rs#301)            root: root.as_ref().to_path_buf(),
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        }
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    }
[304](https://docs.rs#304)
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    /// Set the minimum depth of entries yielded by the iterator.
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    ///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// The smallest depth is `0` and always corresponds to the path given
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    /// to the `new` function on this type. Its direct descendents have depth
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// `1`, and their descendents have depth `2`, and so on.
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    pub fn min_depth(mut self, depth: usize) -> Self {
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        self.opts.min_depth = depth;
[312](https://docs.rs#312)        if self.opts.min_depth > self.opts.max_depth {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)            self.opts.min_depth = self.opts.max_depth;
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        }
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        self
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    }
[317](https://docs.rs#317)
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    /// Set the maximum depth of entries yield by the iterator.
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    ///
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    /// The smallest depth is `0` and always corresponds to the path given
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    /// to the `new` function on this type. Its direct descendents have depth
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    /// `1`, and their descendents have depth `2`, and so on.
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    ///
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    /// Note that this will not simply filter the entries of the iterator, but
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    /// it will actually avoid descending into directories when the depth is
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    /// exceeded.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    pub fn max_depth(mut self, depth: usize) -> Self {
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        self.opts.max_depth = depth;
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        if self.opts.max_depth < self.opts.min_depth {
[330](https://docs.rs#330)            self.opts.max_depth = self.opts.min_depth;
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        self
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    }
[334](https://docs.rs#334)
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    /// Follow symbolic links. By default, this is disabled.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    ///
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// When `yes` is `true`, symbolic links are followed as if they were
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    /// normal directories and files. If a symbolic link is broken or is
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// involved in a loop, an error is yielded.
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    ///
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// When enabled, the yielded [`DirEntry`] values represent the target of
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// the link while the path corresponds to the link. See the [`DirEntry`]
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// type for more details.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    ///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// [`DirEntry`]: struct.DirEntry.html
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    pub fn follow_links(mut self, yes: bool) -> Self {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        self.opts.follow_links = yes;
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        self
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    }
[350](https://docs.rs#350)
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// Follow symbolic links if these are the root of the traversal.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    /// By default, this is enabled.
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    ///
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// When `yes` is `true`, symbolic links on root paths are followed
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    /// which is effective if the symbolic link points to a directory.
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    /// If a symbolic link is broken or is involved in a loop, an error is yielded
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    /// as the first entry of the traversal.
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    ///
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    /// When enabled, the yielded [`DirEntry`] values represent the target of
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// the link while the path corresponds to the link. See the [`DirEntry`]
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// type for more details, and all future entries will be contained within
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    /// the resolved directory behind the symbolic link of the root path.
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    ///
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// [`DirEntry`]: struct.DirEntry.html
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    pub fn follow_root_links(mut self, yes: bool) -> Self {
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        self.opts.follow_root_links = yes;
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        self
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    }
[369](https://docs.rs#369)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    /// Set the maximum number of simultaneously open file descriptors used
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// by the iterator.
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    ///
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// `n` must be greater than or equal to `1`. If `n` is `0`, then it is set
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    /// to `1` automatically. If this is not set, then it defaults to some
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    /// reasonably low number.
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    ///
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    /// This setting has no impact on the results yielded by the iterator
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// (even when `n` is `1`). Instead, this setting represents a trade off
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    /// between scarce resources (file descriptors) and memory. Namely, when
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// the maximum number of file descriptors is reached and a new directory
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// needs to be opened to continue iteration, then a previous directory
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    /// handle is closed and has its unyielded entries stored in memory. In
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    /// practice, this is a satisfying trade off because it scales with respect
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// to the *depth* of your file tree. Therefore, low values (even `1`) are
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    /// acceptable.
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    ///
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// Note that this value does not impact the number of system calls made by
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    /// an exhausted iterator.
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    ///
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    /// # Platform behavior
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    ///
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// On Windows, if `follow_links` is enabled, then this limit is not
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// respected. In particular, the maximum number of file descriptors opened
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// is proportional to the depth of the directory tree traversed.
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    pub fn max_open(mut self, mut n: usize) -> Self {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)        if n == 0 {
[397](https://docs.rs#397)            n = 1;
[398](https://docs.rs#398)        }
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        self.opts.max_open = n;
[400](https://docs.rs#400)        self
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    }
[402](https://docs.rs#402)
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// Set a function for sorting directory entries with a comparator
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    /// function.
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    ///
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// If a compare function is set, the resulting iterator will return all
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// paths in sorted order. The compare function will be called to compare
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// entries from the same directory.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    ///
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// ```rust,no_run
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    /// use std::cmp;
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// use std::ffi::OsString;
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    ///
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// WalkDir::new("foo").sort_by(|a,b| a.file_name().cmp(b.file_name()));
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// ```
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    pub fn sort_by<F>(mut self, cmp: F) -> Self
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    where
[419](https://docs.rs#419)        F: FnMut(&DirEntry, &DirEntry) -> Ordering + Send + Sync + 'static,
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    {
[421](https://docs.rs#421)        self.opts.sorter = Some(Box::new(cmp));
[422](https://docs.rs#422)        self
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    }
[424](https://docs.rs#424)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// Set a function for sorting directory entries with a key extraction
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// function.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// If a compare function is set, the resulting iterator will return all
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// paths in sorted order. The compare function will be called to compare
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// entries from the same directory.
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    ///
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// ```rust,no_run
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// use std::cmp;
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// use std::ffi::OsString;
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    ///
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// WalkDir::new("foo").sort_by_key(|a| a.file_name().to_owned());
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// ```
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    pub fn sort_by_key<K, F>(self, mut cmp: F) -> Self
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    where
[441](https://docs.rs#441)        F: FnMut(&DirEntry) -> K + Send + Sync + 'static,
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        K: Ord,
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    {
[444](https://docs.rs#444)        self.sort_by(move |a, b| cmp(a).cmp(&cmp(b)))
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    }
[446](https://docs.rs#446)
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    /// Sort directory entries by file name, to ensure a deterministic order.
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    ///
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// This is a convenience function for calling `Self::sort_by()`.
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    ///

[458](https://docs.rs#458)    }
[459](https://docs.rs#459)
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// Yield a directory's contents before the directory itself. By default,
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    /// this is disabled.
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    ///
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    /// When `yes` is `false` (as is the default), the directory is yielded
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    /// before its contents are read. This is useful when, e.g. you want to
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    /// skip processing of some directories.
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    ///
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// When `yes` is `true`, the iterator yields the contents of a directory
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    /// before yielding the directory itself. This is useful when, e.g. you
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    /// want to recursively delete a directory.
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    ///
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    /// # Example
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    ///
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    /// Assume the following directory tree:
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    ///
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    /// ```text
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    /// foo/
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    ///   abc/
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    ///     qrs
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    ///     tuv
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    ///   def/
[481](https://docs.rs#481)    /// ```
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    ///
[483](https://docs.rs#483)    /// With contents_first disabled (the default), the following code visits
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    /// the directory tree in depth-first order:
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    ///
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    /// ```no_run
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    /// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    ///
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    /// for entry in WalkDir::new("foo") {
[490](https://docs.rs#490)    ///     let entry = entry.unwrap();
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    ///     println!("{}", entry.path().display());
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    /// }
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    ///
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    /// // foo
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    /// // foo/abc
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    /// // foo/abc/qrs
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    /// // foo/abc/tuv
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    /// // foo/def
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    /// ```
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    ///
[501](https://docs.rs#501)    /// With contents_first enabled:
[502](https://docs.rs#502)    ///
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    /// ```no_run
[504](https://docs.rs#504)    /// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    ///
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    /// for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").contents_first(true) {
[507](https://docs.rs#507)    ///     let entry = entry.unwrap();
[508](https://docs.rs#508)    ///     println!("{}", entry.path().display());
[509](https://docs.rs#509)    /// }
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    ///
[511](https://docs.rs#511)    /// // foo/abc/qrs
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    /// // foo/abc/tuv
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    /// // foo/abc
[514](https://docs.rs#514)    /// // foo/def
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    /// // foo
[516](https://docs.rs#516)    /// ```
[517](https://docs.rs#517)    pub fn contents_first(mut self, yes: bool) -> Self {
[518](https://docs.rs#518)        self.opts.contents_first = yes;
[519](https://docs.rs#519)        self
[520](https://docs.rs#520)    }
[521](https://docs.rs#521)
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    /// Do not cross file system boundaries.
[523](https://docs.rs#523)    ///
[524](https://docs.rs#524)    /// When this option is enabled, directory traversal will not descend into
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    /// directories that are on a different file system from the root path.
[526](https://docs.rs#526)    ///
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    /// Currently, this option is only supported on Unix and Windows. If this
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    /// option is used on an unsupported platform, then directory traversal
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    /// will immediately return an error and will not yield any entries.
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    pub fn same_file_system(mut self, yes: bool) -> Self {
[531](https://docs.rs#531)        self.opts.same_file_system = yes;
[532](https://docs.rs#532)        self
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    }
