[280](https://docs.rs#280)
[281](https://docs.rs#281)impl WalkDir {
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// Create a builder for a recursive directory iterator starting at the
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    /// file path `root`. If `root` is a directory, then it is the first item
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// yielded by the iterator. If `root` is a file, then it is the first
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    /// and only item yielded by the iterator. If `root` is a symlink, then it
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// is always followed for the purposes of directory traversal. (A root
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    /// `DirEntry` still obeys its documentation with respect to symlinks and
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// the `follow_links` setting.)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    pub fn new<P: AsRef<Path>>(root: P) -> Self {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        WalkDir {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)            opts: WalkDirOptions {
[292](https://docs.rs#292)                follow_links: false,
[293](https://docs.rs#293)                follow_root_links: true,
[294](https://docs.rs#294)                max_open: 10,
[295](https://docs.rs#295)                min_depth: 0,
[296](https://docs.rs#296)                max_depth: ::std::usize::MAX,
[297](https://docs.rs#297)                sorter: None,
[298](https://docs.rs#298)                contents_first: false,
[299](https://docs.rs#299)                same_file_system: false,
[300](https://docs.rs#300)            },
[301](https://docs.rs#301)            root: root.as_ref().to_path_buf(),
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        }
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    }
[304](https://docs.rs#304)
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    /// Set the minimum depth of entries yielded by the iterator.
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    ///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// The smallest depth is `0` and always corresponds to the path given
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    /// to the `new` function on this type. Its direct descendents have depth
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// `1`, and their descendents have depth `2`, and so on.
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    pub fn min_depth(mut self, depth: usize) -> Self {
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        self.opts.min_depth = depth;
[312](https://docs.rs#312)        if self.opts.min_depth > self.opts.max_depth {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)            self.opts.min_depth = self.opts.max_depth;
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        }
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        self
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    }
[317](https://docs.rs#317)
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    /// Set the maximum depth of entries yield by the iterator.
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    ///
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    /// The smallest depth is `0` and always corresponds to the path given
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    /// to the `new` function on this type. Its direct descendents have depth
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    /// `1`, and their descendents have depth `2`, and so on.
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    ///
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    /// Note that this will not simply filter the entries of the iterator, but
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    /// it will actually avoid descending into directories when the depth is
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    /// exceeded.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    pub fn max_depth(mut self, depth: usize) -> Self {
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        self.opts.max_depth = depth;
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        if self.opts.max_depth < self.opts.min_depth {
[330](https://docs.rs#330)            self.opts.max_depth = self.opts.min_depth;
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        self
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    }
[334](https://docs.rs#334)
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    /// Follow symbolic links. By default, this is disabled.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    ///
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// When `yes` is `true`, symbolic links are followed as if they were
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    /// normal directories and files. If a symbolic link is broken or is
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// involved in a loop, an error is yielded.
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    ///
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// When enabled, the yielded [`DirEntry`] values represent the target of
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// the link while the path corresponds to the link. See the [`DirEntry`]
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// type for more details.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    ///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// [`DirEntry`]: struct.DirEntry.html
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    pub fn follow_links(mut self, yes: bool) -> Self {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        self.opts.follow_links = yes;
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        self
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    }
[350](https://docs.rs#350)
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// Follow symbolic links if these are the root of the traversal.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    /// By default, this is enabled.
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    ///
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// When `yes` is `true`, symbolic links on root paths are followed
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    /// which is effective if the symbolic link points to a directory.
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    /// If a symbolic link is broken or is involved in a loop, an error is yielded
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    /// as the first entry of the traversal.
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    ///
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    /// When enabled, the yielded [`DirEntry`] values represent the target of
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// the link while the path corresponds to the link. See the [`DirEntry`]
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// type for more details, and all future entries will be contained within
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    /// the resolved directory behind the symbolic link of the root path.
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    ///
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// [`DirEntry`]: struct.DirEntry.html
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    pub fn follow_root_links(mut self, yes: bool) -> Self {
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        self.opts.follow_root_links = yes;
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        self
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    }
[369](https://docs.rs#369)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    /// Set the maximum number of simultaneously open file descriptors used
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// by the iterator.
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    ///
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// `n` must be greater than or equal to `1`. If `n` is `0`, then it is set
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    /// to `1` automatically. If this is not set, then it defaults to some
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    /// reasonably low number.
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    ///
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    /// This setting has no impact on the results yielded by the iterator
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// (even when `n` is `1`). Instead, this setting represents a trade off
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    /// between scarce resources (file descriptors) and memory. Namely, when
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// the maximum number of file descriptors is reached and a new directory
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// needs to be opened to continue iteration, then a previous directory
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    /// handle is closed and has its unyielded entries stored in memory. In
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    /// practice, this is a satisfying trade off because it scales with respect
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// to the *depth* of your file tree. Therefore, low values (even `1`) are
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    /// acceptable.
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    ///
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// Note that this value does not impact the number of system calls made by
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    /// an exhausted iterator.
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    ///
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    /// # Platform behavior
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    ///
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// On Windows, if `follow_links` is enabled, then this limit is not
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// respected. In particular, the maximum number of file descriptors opened
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// is proportional to the depth of the directory tree traversed.
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    pub fn max_open(mut self, mut n: usize) -> Self {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)        if n == 0 {
[397](https://docs.rs#397)            n = 1;
[398](https://docs.rs#398)        }
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        self.opts.max_open = n;
[400](https://docs.rs#400)        self
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    }
[402](https://docs.rs#402)
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// Set a function for sorting directory entries with a comparator
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    /// function.
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    ///
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// If a compare function is set, the resulting iterator will return all
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// paths in sorted order. The compare function will be called to compare
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// entries from the same directory.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    ///
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// ```rust,no_run
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    /// use std::cmp;
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// use std::ffi::OsString;
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    ///
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// WalkDir::new("foo").sort_by(|a,b| a.file_name().cmp(b.file_name()));
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// ```
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    pub fn sort_by<F>(mut self, cmp: F) -> Self
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    where
[419](https://docs.rs#419)        F: FnMut(&DirEntry, &DirEntry) -> Ordering + Send + Sync + 'static,
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    {
[421](https://docs.rs#421)        self.opts.sorter = Some(Box::new(cmp));
[422](https://docs.rs#422)        self
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    }
[424](https://docs.rs#424)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// Set a function for sorting directory entries with a key extraction
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// function.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// If a compare function is set, the resulting iterator will return all
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// paths in sorted order. The compare function will be called to compare
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// entries from the same directory.
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    ///
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// ```rust,no_run
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// use std::cmp;
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// use std::ffi::OsString;
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    ///
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// WalkDir::new("foo").sort_by_key(|a| a.file_name().to_owned());
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// ```
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    pub fn sort_by_key<K, F>(self, mut cmp: F) -> Self
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    where
[441](https://docs.rs#441)        F: FnMut(&DirEntry) -> K + Send + Sync + 'static,
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        K: Ord,
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    {
[444](https://docs.rs#444)        self.sort_by(move |a, b| cmp(a).cmp(&cmp(b)))
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    }
[446](https://docs.rs#446)
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    /// Sort directory entries by file name, to ensure a deterministic order.
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    ///
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// This is a convenience function for calling `Self::sort_by()`.
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    ///
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// ```rust,no_run
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    /// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    ///
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// WalkDir::new("foo").sort_by_file_name();
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    /// ```
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    pub fn sort_by_file_name(self) -> Self {
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        self.sort_by(|a, b| a.file_name().cmp(b.file_name()))
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    }
[459](https://docs.rs#459)
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// Yield a directory's contents before the directory itself. By default,
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    /// this is disabled.
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    ///
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    /// When `yes` is `false` (as is the default), the directory is yielded
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    /// before its contents are read. This is useful when, e.g. you want to
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    /// skip processing of some directories.
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    ///
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// When `yes` is `true`, the iterator yields the contents of a directory
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    /// before yielding the directory itself. This is useful when, e.g. you
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    /// want to recursively delete a directory.
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    ///
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    /// # Example
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    ///
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    /// Assume the following directory tree:
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    ///
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    /// ```text
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    /// foo/
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    ///   abc/
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    ///     qrs
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    ///     tuv
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    ///   def/
[481](https://docs.rs#481)    /// ```
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    ///
[483](https://docs.rs#483)    /// With contents_first disabled (the default), the following code visits
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    /// the directory tree in depth-first order:
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    ///
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    /// ```no_run
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    /// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    ///
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    /// for entry in WalkDir::new("foo") {
[490](https://docs.rs#490)    ///     let entry = entry.unwrap();
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    ///     println!("{}", entry.path().display());
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    /// }
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    ///
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    /// // foo
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    /// // foo/abc
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    /// // foo/abc/qrs
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    /// // foo/abc/tuv
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    /// // foo/def
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    /// ```
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    ///
[501](https://docs.rs#501)    /// With contents_first enabled:
[502](https://docs.rs#502)    ///
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    /// ```no_run
[504](https://docs.rs#504)    /// use walkdir::WalkDir;
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    ///
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    /// for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").contents_first(true) {
[507](https://docs.rs#507)    ///     let entry = entry.unwrap();
[508](https://docs.rs#508)    ///     println!("{}", entry.path().display());
[509](https://docs.rs#509)    /// }
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    ///
[511](https://docs.rs#511)    /// // foo/abc/qrs
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    /// // foo/abc/tuv
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    /// // foo/abc
[514](https://docs.rs#514)    /// // foo/def
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    /// // foo
[516](https://docs.rs#516)    /// ```
[517](https://docs.rs#517)    pub fn contents_first(mut self, yes: bool) -> Self {
[518](https://docs.rs#518)        self.opts.contents_first = yes;
[519](https://docs.rs#519)        self
[520](https://docs.rs#520)    }
[521](https://docs.rs#521)
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    /// Do not cross file system boundaries.
[523](https://docs.rs#523)    ///
[524](https://docs.rs#524)    /// When this option is enabled, directory traversal will not descend into
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    /// directories that are on a different file system from the root path.
[526](https://docs.rs#526)    ///
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    /// Currently, this option is only supported on Unix and Windows. If this
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    /// option is used on an unsupported platform, then directory traversal
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    /// will immediately return an error and will not yield any entries.
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    pub fn same_file_system(mut self, yes: bool) -> Self {
[531](https://docs.rs#531)        self.opts.same_file_system = yes;
[532](https://docs.rs#532)        self
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    }

[553](https://docs.rs#553)
[554](https://docs.rs#554)/// An iterator for recursively descending into a directory.
[555](https://docs.rs#555)///
[556](https://docs.rs#556)/// A value with this type must be constructed with the [`WalkDir`] type, which
[557](https://docs.rs#557)/// uses a builder pattern to set options such as min/max depth, max open file
[558](https://docs.rs#558)/// descriptors and whether the iterator should follow symbolic links. After
[559](https://docs.rs#559)/// constructing a `WalkDir`, call [`.into_iter()`] at the end of the chain.
[560](https://docs.rs#560)///
[561](https://docs.rs#561)/// The order of elements yielded by this iterator is unspecified.
[562](https://docs.rs#562)///
[563](https://docs.rs#563)/// [`WalkDir`]: struct.WalkDir.html
[564](https://docs.rs#564)/// [`.into_iter()`]: struct.WalkDir.html#into_iter.v
[565](https://docs.rs#565)#[derive(Debug)]
[566](https://docs.rs#566)pub struct IntoIter {
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    /// Options specified in the builder. Depths, max fds, etc.
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    opts: WalkDirOptions,
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    /// The start path.
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    ///
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    /// This is only `Some(...)` at the beginning. After the first iteration,
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    /// this is always `None`.
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    start: Option<PathBuf>,
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    /// A stack of open (up to max fd) or closed handles to directories.
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    /// An open handle is a plain [`fs::ReadDir`] while a closed handle is
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    /// a `Vec<fs::DirEntry>` corresponding to the as-of-yet consumed entries.
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    ///
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    /// [`fs::ReadDir`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/fs/struct.ReadDir.html
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    stack_list: Vec<DirList>,
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// A stack of file paths.
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    ///
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    /// This is *only* used when [`follow_links`] is enabled. In all other
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    /// cases this stack is empty.
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    ///
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    /// [`follow_links`]: struct.WalkDir.html#method.follow_links
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    stack_path: Vec<Ancestor>,
[587](https://docs.rs#587)    /// An index into `stack_list` that points to the oldest open directory
[588](https://docs.rs#588)    /// handle. If the maximum fd limit is reached and a new directory needs to
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    /// be read, the handle at this index is closed before the new directory is
[590](https://docs.rs#590)    /// opened.
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    oldest_opened: usize,
[592](https://docs.rs#592)    /// The current depth of iteration (the length of the stack at the
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    /// beginning of each iteration).
[594](https://docs.rs#594)    depth: usize,
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    /// A list of DirEntries corresponding to directories, that are
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    /// yielded after their contents has been fully yielded. This is only
[597](https://docs.rs#597)    /// used when `contents_first` is enabled.
[598](https://docs.rs#598)    deferred_dirs: Vec<DirEntry>,
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    /// The device of the root file path when the first call to `next` was
[600](https://docs.rs#600)    /// made.
[601](https://docs.rs#601)    ///
[602](https://docs.rs#602)    /// If the `same_file_system` option isn't enabled, then this is always
[603](https://docs.rs#603)    /// `None`. Conversely, if it is enabled, this is always `Some(...)` after
[604](https://docs.rs#604)    /// handling the root path.
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    root_device: Option<u64>,
[606](https://docs.rs#606)}
[607](https://docs.rs#607)
[608](https://docs.rs#608)/// An ancestor is an item in the directory tree traversed by walkdir, and is
[609](https://docs.rs#609)/// used to check for loops in the tree when traversing symlinks.
[610](https://docs.rs#610)#[derive(Debug)]
[611](https://docs.rs#611)struct Ancestor {
[612](https://docs.rs#612)    /// The path of this ancestor.
[613](https://docs.rs#613)    path: PathBuf,
[614](https://docs.rs#614)    /// An open file to this ancesor. This is only used on Windows where
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    /// opening a file handle appears to be quite expensive, so we choose to
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    /// cache it. This comes at the cost of not respecting the file descriptor
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    /// limit set by the user.
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    #[cfg(windows)]
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    handle: Handle,
[620](https://docs.rs#620)}
[621](https://docs.rs#621)
[622](https://docs.rs#622)impl Ancestor {
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    /// Create a new ancestor from the given directory path.
[624](https://docs.rs#624)    #[cfg(windows)]
[625](https://docs.rs#625)    fn new(dent: &DirEntry) -> io::Result<Ancestor> {
[626](https://docs.rs#626)        let handle = Handle::from_path(dent.path())?;
[627](https://docs.rs#627)        Ok(Ancestor { path: dent.path().to_path_buf(), handle })
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    }
[629](https://docs.rs#629)
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    /// Create a new ancestor from the given directory path.
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    #[cfg(not(windows))]
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    fn new(dent: &DirEntry) -> io::Result<Ancestor> {
[633](https://docs.rs#633)        Ok(Ancestor { path: dent.path().to_path_buf() })
[634](https://docs.rs#634)    }
[635](https://docs.rs#635)
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    /// Returns true if and only if the given open file handle corresponds to
[637](https://docs.rs#637)    /// the same directory as this ancestor.
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    #[cfg(windows)]
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    fn is_same(&self, child: &Handle) -> io::Result<bool> {
[640](https://docs.rs#640)        Ok(child == &self.handle)
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    }
[642](https://docs.rs#642)
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    /// Returns true if and only if the given open file handle corresponds to
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    /// the same directory as this ancestor.
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    #[cfg(not(windows))]
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    fn is_same(&self, child: &Handle) -> io::Result<bool> {
[647](https://docs.rs#647)        Ok(child == &Handle::from_path(&self.path)?)
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    }
[649](https://docs.rs#649)}
[650](https://docs.rs#650)
[651](https://docs.rs#651)/// A sequence of unconsumed directory entries.
[652](https://docs.rs#652)///
[653](https://docs.rs#653)/// This represents the opened or closed state of a directory handle. When
[654](https://docs.rs#654)/// open, future entries are read by iterating over the raw `fs::ReadDir`.
[655](https://docs.rs#655)/// When closed, all future entries are read into memory. Iteration then
[656](https://docs.rs#656)/// proceeds over a [`Vec<fs::DirEntry>`].
[657](https://docs.rs#657)///
[658](https://docs.rs#658)/// [`fs::ReadDir`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/fs/struct.ReadDir.html
[659](https://docs.rs#659)/// [`Vec<fs::DirEntry>`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/vec/struct.Vec.html
[660](https://docs.rs#660)#[derive(Debug)]
[661](https://docs.rs#661)enum DirList {
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    /// An opened handle.
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    ///
[664](https://docs.rs#664)    /// This includes the depth of the handle itself.
[665](https://docs.rs#665)    ///
[666](https://docs.rs#666)    /// If there was an error with the initial [`fs::read_dir`] call, then it
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    /// is stored here. (We use an [`Option<...>`] to make yielding the error
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    /// exactly once simpler.)
[669](https://docs.rs#669)    ///
[670](https://docs.rs#670)    /// [`fs::read_dir`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/fs/fn.read_dir.html
[671](https://docs.rs#671)    /// [`Option<...>`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/option/enum.Option.html
[672](https://docs.rs#672)    Opened { depth: usize, it: result::Result<ReadDir, Option<Error>> },
[673](https://docs.rs#673)    /// A closed handle.
[674](https://docs.rs#674)    ///
[675](https://docs.rs#675)    /// All remaining directory entries are read into memory.
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    Closed(vec::IntoIter<Result<DirEntry>>),
[677](https://docs.rs#677)}
[678](https://docs.rs#678)
[679](https://docs.rs#679)impl Iterator for IntoIter {
[680](https://docs.rs#680)    type Item = Result<DirEntry>;
[681](https://docs.rs#681)    /// Advances the iterator and returns the next value.
[682](https://docs.rs#682)    ///
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    /// # Errors
[684](https://docs.rs#684)    ///
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    /// If the iterator fails to retrieve the next value, this method returns
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    /// an error value. The error will be wrapped in an Option::Some.
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Result<DirEntry>> {
[688](https://docs.rs#688)        if let Some(start) = self.start.take() {
[689](https://docs.rs#689)            if self.opts.same_file_system {
[690](https://docs.rs#690)                let result = util::device_num(&start)
[691](https://docs.rs#691)                    .map_err(|e| Error::from_path(0, start.clone(), e));
[692](https://docs.rs#692)                self.root_device = Some(itry!(result));
[693](https://docs.rs#693)            }
[694](https://docs.rs#694)            let dent = itry!(DirEntry::from_path(0, start, false));
[695](https://docs.rs#695)            if let Some(result) = self.handle_entry(dent) {
[696](https://docs.rs#696)                return Some(result);
[697](https://docs.rs#697)            }
[698](https://docs.rs#698)        }
[699](https://docs.rs#699)        while !self.stack_list.is_empty() {
[700](https://docs.rs#700)            self.depth = self.stack_list.len();
[701](https://docs.rs#701)            if let Some(dentry) = self.get_deferred_dir() {
[702](https://docs.rs#702)                return Some(Ok(dentry));
[703](https://docs.rs#703)            }
[704](https://docs.rs#704)            if self.depth > self.opts.max_depth {
[705](https://docs.rs#705)                // If we've exceeded the max depth, pop the current dir
[706](https://docs.rs#706)                // so that we don't descend.
[707](https://docs.rs#707)                self.pop();
[708](https://docs.rs#708)                continue;
[709](https://docs.rs#709)            }
[710](https://docs.rs#710)            // Unwrap is safe here because we've verified above that
[711](https://docs.rs#711)            // `self.stack_list` is not empty
[712](https://docs.rs#712)            let next = self
[713](https://docs.rs#713)                .stack_list
[714](https://docs.rs#714)                .last_mut()
[715](https://docs.rs#715)                .expect("BUG: stack should be non-empty")
[716](https://docs.rs#716)                .next();
[717](https://docs.rs#717)            match next {
[718](https://docs.rs#718)                None => self.pop(),
[719](https://docs.rs#719)                Some(Err(err)) => return Some(Err(err)),
[720](https://docs.rs#720)                Some(Ok(dent)) => {
[721](https://docs.rs#721)                    if let Some(result) = self.handle_entry(dent) {
[722](https://docs.rs#722)                        return Some(result);
[723](https://docs.rs#723)                    }
[724](https://docs.rs#724)                }
[725](https://docs.rs#725)            }
[726](https://docs.rs#726)        }
[727](https://docs.rs#727)        if self.opts.contents_first {
[728](https://docs.rs#728)            self.depth = self.stack_list.len();
[729](https://docs.rs#729)            if let Some(dentry) = self.get_deferred_dir() {
[730](https://docs.rs#730)                return Some(Ok(dentry));
[731](https://docs.rs#731)            }
[732](https://docs.rs#732)        }
[733](https://docs.rs#733)        None
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    }
[735](https://docs.rs#735)}
[736](https://docs.rs#736)
[737](https://docs.rs#737)impl IntoIter {
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    /// Skips the current directory.
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    ///
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    /// This causes the iterator to stop traversing the contents of the least
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    /// recently yielded directory. This means any remaining entries in that
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    /// directory will be skipped (including sub-directories).
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    ///
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    /// Note that the ergonomics of this method are questionable since it
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    /// borrows the iterator mutably. Namely, you must write out the looping
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    /// condition manually. For example, to skip hidden entries efficiently on
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    /// unix systems:
[748](https://docs.rs#748)    ///
[749](https://docs.rs#749)    /// ```no_run
[750](https://docs.rs#750)    /// use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
[751](https://docs.rs#751)    ///
[752](https://docs.rs#752)    /// fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    ///     entry.file_name()
[754](https://docs.rs#754)    ///          .to_str()
[755](https://docs.rs#755)    ///          .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
[756](https://docs.rs#756)    ///          .unwrap_or(false)
[757](https://docs.rs#757)    /// }
[758](https://docs.rs#758)    ///
[759](https://docs.rs#759)    /// let mut it = WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter();
[760](https://docs.rs#760)    /// loop {
[761](https://docs.rs#761)    ///     let entry = match it.next() {
[762](https://docs.rs#762)    ///         None => break,
[763](https://docs.rs#763)    ///         Some(Err(err)) => panic!("ERROR: {}", err),
[764](https://docs.rs#764)    ///         Some(Ok(entry)) => entry,
[765](https://docs.rs#765)    ///     };
[766](https://docs.rs#766)    ///     if is_hidden(&entry) {
[767](https://docs.rs#767)    ///         if entry.file_type().is_dir() {
[768](https://docs.rs#768)    ///             it.skip_current_dir();
[769](https://docs.rs#769)    ///         }
[770](https://docs.rs#770)    ///         continue;
[771](https://docs.rs#771)    ///     }
[772](https://docs.rs#772)    ///     println!("{}", entry.path().display());
[773](https://docs.rs#773)    /// }
[774](https://docs.rs#774)    /// ```
[775](https://docs.rs#775)    ///
[776](https://docs.rs#776)    /// You may find it more convenient to use the [`filter_entry`] iterator
[777](https://docs.rs#777)    /// adapter. (See its documentation for the same example functionality as
[778](https://docs.rs#778)    /// above.)
[779](https://docs.rs#779)    ///
[780](https://docs.rs#780)    /// [`filter_entry`]: #method.filter_entry
[781](https://docs.rs#781)    pub fn skip_current_dir(&mut self) {
[782](https://docs.rs#782)        if !self.stack_list.is_empty() {
[783](https://docs.rs#783)            self.pop();
[784](https://docs.rs#784)        }
[785](https://docs.rs#785)    }
[786](https://docs.rs#786)
[787](https://docs.rs#787)    /// Yields only entries which satisfy the given predicate and skips
[788](https://docs.rs#788)    /// descending into directories that do not satisfy the given predicate.
[789](https://docs.rs#789)    ///
[790](https://docs.rs#790)    /// The predicate is applied to all entries. If the predicate is
[791](https://docs.rs#791)    /// true, iteration carries on as normal. If the predicate is false, the
[792](https://docs.rs#792)    /// entry is ignored and if it is a directory, it is not descended into.
[793](https://docs.rs#793)    ///
[794](https://docs.rs#794)    /// This is often more convenient to use than [`skip_current_dir`]. For
[795](https://docs.rs#795)    /// example, to skip hidden files and directories efficiently on unix
[796](https://docs.rs#796)    /// systems:
[797](https://docs.rs#797)    ///
[798](https://docs.rs#798)    /// ```no_run
[799](https://docs.rs#799)    /// use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
[800](https://docs.rs#800)    /// # use walkdir::Error;
[801](https://docs.rs#801)    ///
[802](https://docs.rs#802)    /// fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
[803](https://docs.rs#803)    ///     entry.file_name()
[804](https://docs.rs#804)    ///          .to_str()
[805](https://docs.rs#805)    ///          .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
[806](https://docs.rs#806)    ///          .unwrap_or(false)
[807](https://docs.rs#807)    /// }
[808](https://docs.rs#808)    ///
[809](https://docs.rs#809)    /// # fn try_main() -> Result<(), Error> {
[810](https://docs.rs#810)    /// for entry in WalkDir::new("foo")
[811](https://docs.rs#811)    ///                      .into_iter()
[812](https://docs.rs#812)    ///                      .filter_entry(|e| !is_hidden(e)) {
[813](https://docs.rs#813)    ///     println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
[814](https://docs.rs#814)    /// }
[815](https://docs.rs#815)    /// # Ok(())
[816](https://docs.rs#816)    /// # }
[817](https://docs.rs#817)    /// ```
[818](https://docs.rs#818)    ///
[819](https://docs.rs#819)    /// Note that the iterator will still yield errors for reading entries that
[820](https://docs.rs#820)    /// may not satisfy the predicate.
[821](https://docs.rs#821)    ///
[822](https://docs.rs#822)    /// Note that entries skipped with [`min_depth`] and [`max_depth`] are not
[823](https://docs.rs#823)    /// passed to this predicate.
[824](https://docs.rs#824)    ///
[825](https://docs.rs#825)    /// Note that if the iterator has `contents_first` enabled, then this
[826](https://docs.rs#826)    /// method is no different than calling the standard `Iterator::filter`
[827](https://docs.rs#827)    /// method (because directory entries are yielded after they've been
[828](https://docs.rs#828)    /// descended into).
[829](https://docs.rs#829)    ///
[830](https://docs.rs#830)    /// [`skip_current_dir`]: #method.skip_current_dir
[831](https://docs.rs#831)    /// [`min_depth`]: struct.WalkDir.html#method.min_depth
[832](https://docs.rs#832)    /// [`max_depth`]: struct.WalkDir.html#method.max_depth
[833](https://docs.rs#833)    pub fn filter_entry<P>(self, predicate: P) -> FilterEntry<Self, P>
[834](https://docs.rs#834)    where
[835](https://docs.rs#835)        P: FnMut(&DirEntry) -> bool,
[836](https://docs.rs#836)    {
[837](https://docs.rs#837)        FilterEntry { it: self, predicate }
[838](https://docs.rs#838)    }
[839](https://docs.rs#839)
[840](https://docs.rs#840)    fn handle_entry(
[841](https://docs.rs#841)        &mut self,
[842](https://docs.rs#842)        mut dent: DirEntry,
[843](https://docs.rs#843)    ) -> Option<Result<DirEntry>> {
[844](https://docs.rs#844)        if self.opts.follow_links && dent.file_type().is_symlink() {
[845](https://docs.rs#845)            dent = itry!(self.follow(dent));
[846](https://docs.rs#846)        }
[847](https://docs.rs#847)        let is_normal_dir = !dent.file_type().is_symlink() && dent.is_dir();
[848](https://docs.rs#848)        if is_normal_dir {
[849](https://docs.rs#849)            if self.opts.same_file_system && dent.depth() > 0 {
[850](https://docs.rs#850)                if itry!(self.is_same_file_system(&dent)) {
[851](https://docs.rs#851)                    itry!(self.push(&dent));
[852](https://docs.rs#852)                }
[853](https://docs.rs#853)            } else {
[854](https://docs.rs#854)                itry!(self.push(&dent));
[855](https://docs.rs#855)            }
[856](https://docs.rs#856)        } else if dent.depth() == 0
[857](https://docs.rs#857)            && dent.file_type().is_symlink()
[858](https://docs.rs#858)            && self.opts.follow_root_links
[859](https://docs.rs#859)        {
[860](https://docs.rs#860)            // As a special case, if we are processing a root entry, then we
[861](https://docs.rs#861)            // always follow it even if it's a symlink and follow_links is
[862](https://docs.rs#862)            // false. We are careful to not let this change the semantics of
[863](https://docs.rs#863)            // the DirEntry however. Namely, the DirEntry should still respect
[864](https://docs.rs#864)            // the follow_links setting. When it's disabled, it should report
[865](https://docs.rs#865)            // itself as a symlink. When it's enabled, it should always report
[866](https://docs.rs#866)            // itself as the target.
[867](https://docs.rs#867)            let md = itry!(fs::metadata(dent.path()).map_err(|err| {
[868](https://docs.rs#868)                Error::from_path(dent.depth(), dent.path().to_path_buf(), err)
[869](https://docs.rs#869)            }));
[870](https://docs.rs#870)            if md.file_type().is_dir() {
[871](https://docs.rs#871)                itry!(self.push(&dent));
[872](https://docs.rs#872)            }
[873](https://docs.rs#873)        }
[874](https://docs.rs#874)        if is_normal_dir && self.opts.contents_first {
[875](https://docs.rs#875)            self.deferred_dirs.push(dent);
[876](https://docs.rs#876)            None
[877](https://docs.rs#877)        } else if self.skippable() {
[878](https://docs.rs#878)            None
[879](https://docs.rs#879)        } else {
[880](https://docs.rs#880)            Some(Ok(dent))
[881](https://docs.rs#881)        }
[882](https://docs.rs#882)    }
[883](https://docs.rs#883)
[884](https://docs.rs#884)    fn get_deferred_dir(&mut self) -> Option<DirEntry> {
[885](https://docs.rs#885)        if self.opts.contents_first {
[886](https://docs.rs#886)            if self.depth < self.deferred_dirs.len() {
[887](https://docs.rs#887)                // Unwrap is safe here because we've guaranteed that
[888](https://docs.rs#888)                // `self.deferred_dirs.len()` can never be less than 1
[889](https://docs.rs#889)                let deferred: DirEntry = self
[890](https://docs.rs#890)                    .deferred_dirs
[891](https://docs.rs#891)                    .pop()
[892](https://docs.rs#892)                    .expect("BUG: deferred_dirs should be non-empty");
[893](https://docs.rs#893)                if !self.skippable() {
[894](https://docs.rs#894)                    return Some(deferred);
[895](https://docs.rs#895)                }
[896](https://docs.rs#896)            }
[897](https://docs.rs#897)        }
[898](https://docs.rs#898)        None
[899](https://docs.rs#899)    }
[900](https://docs.rs#900)
[901](https://docs.rs#901)    fn push(&mut self, dent: &DirEntry) -> Result<()> {
[902](https://docs.rs#902)        // Make room for another open file descriptor if we've hit the max.
[903](https://docs.rs#903)        let free =
[904](https://docs.rs#904)            self.stack_list.len().checked_sub(self.oldest_opened).unwrap();
[905](https://docs.rs#905)        if free == self.opts.max_open {
[906](https://docs.rs#906)            self.stack_list[self.oldest_opened].close();
[907](https://docs.rs#907)        }
[908](https://docs.rs#908)        // Open a handle to reading the directory's entries.
[909](https://docs.rs#909)        let rd = fs::read_dir(dent.path()).map_err(|err| {
[910](https://docs.rs#910)            Some(Error::from_path(self.depth, dent.path().to_path_buf(), err))
[911](https://docs.rs#911)        });
[912](https://docs.rs#912)        let mut list = DirList::Opened { depth: self.depth, it: rd };
[913](https://docs.rs#913)        if let Some(ref mut cmp) = self.opts.sorter {
[914](https://docs.rs#914)            let mut entries: Vec<_> = list.collect();
[915](https://docs.rs#915)            entries.sort_by(|a, b| match (a, b) {
[916](https://docs.rs#916)                (&Ok(ref a), &Ok(ref b)) => cmp(a, b),
[917](https://docs.rs#917)                (&Err(_), &Err(_)) => Ordering::Equal,
[918](https://docs.rs#918)                (&Ok(_), &Err(_)) => Ordering::Greater,
[919](https://docs.rs#919)                (&Err(_), &Ok(_)) => Ordering::Less,
[920](https://docs.rs#920)            });
[921](https://docs.rs#921)            list = DirList::Closed(entries.into_iter());
[922](https://docs.rs#922)        }
[923](https://docs.rs#923)        if self.opts.follow_links {
[924](https://docs.rs#924)            let ancestor = Ancestor::new(&dent)
[925](https://docs.rs#925)                .map_err(|err| Error::from_io(self.depth, err))?;
[926](https://docs.rs#926)            self.stack_path.push(ancestor);
[927](https://docs.rs#927)        }
[928](https://docs.rs#928)        // We push this after stack_path since creating the Ancestor can fail.
[929](https://docs.rs#929)        // If it fails, then we return the error and won't descend.
[930](https://docs.rs#930)        self.stack_list.push(list);
[931](https://docs.rs#931)        // If we had to close out a previous directory stream, then we need to
[932](https://docs.rs#932)        // increment our index the oldest still-open stream. We do this only
[933](https://docs.rs#933)        // after adding to our stack, in order to ensure that the oldest_opened
[934](https://docs.rs#934)        // index remains valid. The worst that can happen is that an already
[935](https://docs.rs#935)        // closed stream will be closed again, which is a no-op.
[936](https://docs.rs#936)        //
[937](https://docs.rs#937)        // We could move the close of the stream above into this if-body, but
[938](https://docs.rs#938)        // then we would have more than the maximum number of file descriptors
[939](https://docs.rs#939)        // open at a particular point in time.
[940](https://docs.rs#940)        if free == self.opts.max_open {
[941](https://docs.rs#941)            // Unwrap is safe here because self.oldest_opened is guaranteed to
[942](https://docs.rs#942)            // never be greater than `self.stack_list.len()`, which implies
[943](https://docs.rs#943)            // that the subtraction won't underflow and that adding 1 will
[944](https://docs.rs#944)            // never overflow.
[945](https://docs.rs#945)            self.oldest_opened = self.oldest_opened.checked_add(1).unwrap();
[946](https://docs.rs#946)        }
[947](https://docs.rs#947)        Ok(())
[948](https://docs.rs#948)    }
[949](https://docs.rs#949)
[950](https://docs.rs#950)    fn pop(&mut self) {
[951](https://docs.rs#951)        self.stack_list.pop().expect("BUG: cannot pop from empty stack");
[952](https://docs.rs#952)        if self.opts.follow_links {
[953](https://docs.rs#953)            self.stack_path.pop().expect("BUG: list/path stacks out of sync");
[954](https://docs.rs#954)        }
[955](https://docs.rs#955)        // If everything in the stack is already closed, then there is
[956](https://docs.rs#956)        // room for at least one more open descriptor and it will
[957](https://docs.rs#957)        // always be at the top of the stack.
[958](https://docs.rs#958)        self.oldest_opened = min(self.oldest_opened, self.stack_list.len());
[959](https://docs.rs#959)    }

# WalkDir in walkdir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/walkdir/latest/target-redirect/walkdir/struct.WalkDir.html

`pub struct WalkDir { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A builder to create an iterator for recursively walking a directory.

Results are returned in depth first fashion, with directories yielded
before their contents. If [ contents_first](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.contents_first) is true, contents are yielded
before their directories. The order is unspecified but if

[is given, directory entries are sorted according to this function. Directory entries](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.sort_by)

`sort_by``.` and `..` are always omitted.If an error occurs at any point during iteration, then it is returned in place of its corresponding directory entry and iteration continues as normal. If an error occurs while opening a directory for reading, then it is not descended into (but the error is still yielded by the iterator). Iteration may be stopped at any time. When the iterator is destroyed, all resources associated with it are freed.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

This type implements [ IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/iter/trait.IntoIterator.html) so that it may be used as the subject
of a

`for` loop. You may need to call [explicitly if you want to use iterator adapters such as](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/trait.IntoIterator.html#tymethod.into_iter)

`into_iter`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html#method.filter_entry)

`filter_entry`Idiomatic use of this type should use method chaining to set desired
options. For example, this only shows entries with a depth of `1`, `2` or
`3` (relative to `foo`):

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").min_depth(1).max_depth(3) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
Note that the iterator by default includes the top-most directory. Since
this is the only directory yielded with depth `0`, it is easy to ignore it
with the [ min_depth](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.min_depth) setting:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").min_depth(1) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
This will only return descendents of the `foo` directory and not `foo`
itself.

[§](https://docs.rs#loops)Loops

This iterator (like most/all recursive directory iterators) assumes that
no loops can be made with *hard* links on your file system. In particular,
this would require creating a hard link to a directory such that it creates
a loop. On most platforms, this operation is illegal.

Note that when following symbolic/soft links, loops are detected and an error is reported.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a builder for a recursive directory iterator starting at the
file path `root`. If `root` is a directory, then it is the first item
yielded by the iterator. If `root` is a file, then it is the first
and only item yielded by the iterator. If `root` is a symlink, then it
is always followed for the purposes of directory traversal. (A root
`DirEntry` still obeys its documentation with respect to symlinks and
the `follow_links` setting.)

Set the minimum depth of entries yielded by the iterator.

The smallest depth is `0` and always corresponds to the path given
to the `new` function on this type. Its direct descendents have depth
`1`, and their descendents have depth `2`, and so on.

Set the maximum depth of entries yield by the iterator.

The smallest depth is `0` and always corresponds to the path given
to the `new` function on this type. Its direct descendents have depth
`1`, and their descendents have depth `2`, and so on.

Note that this will not simply filter the entries of the iterator, but it will actually avoid descending into directories when the depth is exceeded.

Follow symbolic links. By default, this is disabled.

When `yes` is `true`, symbolic links are followed as if they were
normal directories and files. If a symbolic link is broken or is
involved in a loop, an error is yielded.

When enabled, the yielded [ DirEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html) values represent the target of
the link while the path corresponds to the link. See the

[type for more details.](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html)

`DirEntry`Follow symbolic links if these are the root of the traversal. By default, this is enabled.

When `yes` is `true`, symbolic links on root paths are followed
which is effective if the symbolic link points to a directory.
If a symbolic link is broken or is involved in a loop, an error is yielded
as the first entry of the traversal.

When enabled, the yielded [ DirEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html) values represent the target of
the link while the path corresponds to the link. See the

[type for more details, and all future entries will be contained within the resolved directory behind the symbolic link of the root path.](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html)

`DirEntry`Set the maximum number of simultaneously open file descriptors used by the iterator.

`n` must be greater than or equal to `1`. If `n` is `0`, then it is set
to `1` automatically. If this is not set, then it defaults to some
reasonably low number.

This setting has no impact on the results yielded by the iterator
(even when `n` is `1`). Instead, this setting represents a trade off
between scarce resources (file descriptors) and memory. Namely, when
the maximum number of file descriptors is reached and a new directory
needs to be opened to continue iteration, then a previous directory
handle is closed and has its unyielded entries stored in memory. In
practice, this is a satisfying trade off because it scales with respect
to the *depth* of your file tree. Therefore, low values (even `1`) are
acceptable.

Note that this value does not impact the number of system calls made by an exhausted iterator.

[§](https://docs.rs#platform-behavior)Platform behavior

On Windows, if `follow_links` is enabled, then this limit is not
respected. In particular, the maximum number of file descriptors opened
is proportional to the depth of the directory tree traversed.

Set a function for sorting directory entries with a comparator function.

If a compare function is set, the resulting iterator will return all paths in sorted order. The compare function will be called to compare entries from the same directory.

```
use std::cmp;
use std::ffi::OsString;
use walkdir::WalkDir;
WalkDir::new("foo").sort_by(|a,b| a.file_name().cmp(b.file_name()));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#517-520)#### pub fn [contents_first](https://docs.rs#method.contents_first)(self, yes: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#517-520)

#### pub fn [contents_first](https://docs.rs#method.contents_first)(self, yes: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

Yield a directory’s contents before the directory itself. By default, this is disabled.

When `yes` is `false` (as is the default), the directory is yielded
before its contents are read. This is useful when, e.g. you want to
skip processing of some directories.

When `yes` is `true`, the iterator yields the contents of a directory
before yielding the directory itself. This is useful when, e.g. you
want to recursively delete a directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Assume the following directory tree:

```
foo/
  abc/
    qrs
    tuv
  def/
```
With contents_first disabled (the default), the following code visits the directory tree in depth-first order:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo") {
    let entry = entry.unwrap();
    println!("{}", entry.path().display());
}
// foo
// foo/abc
// foo/abc/qrs
// foo/abc/tuv
// foo/def
```
With contents_first enabled:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").contents_first(true) {
    let entry = entry.unwrap();
    println!("{}", entry.path().display());
}
// foo/abc/qrs
// foo/abc/tuv
// foo/abc
// foo/def
// foo
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#530-533)#### pub fn [same_file_system](https://docs.rs#method.same_file_system)(self, yes: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#530-533)

#### pub fn [same_file_system](https://docs.rs#method.same_file_system)(self, yes: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

Do not cross file system boundaries.

When this option is enabled, directory traversal will not descend into directories that are on a different file system from the root path.

Currently, this option is only supported on Unix and Windows. If this option is used on an unsupported platform, then directory traversal will immediately return an error and will not yield any entries.

# Error in walkdir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/walkdir/latest/target-redirect/walkdir/struct.Error.html

`pub struct Error { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An error produced by recursively walking a directory.

This error type is a light wrapper around [ std::io::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/struct.Error.html). In
particular, it adds the following information:

- The depth at which the error occurred in the file tree, relative to the root.
- The path, if any, associated with the IO error.
- An indication that a loop occurred when following symbolic links. In this case, there is no underlying IO error.

To maintain good ergonomics, this type has a
[ impl From<Error> for std::io::Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html#impl-From%3CError%3E) defined which preserves the original context.
This allows you to use an

[with methods in this crate if you don’t care about accessing the underlying error data in a structured form.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/type.Result.html)

`io::Result`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Inspect the original [ io::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/struct.Error.html) if there is one.

[ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) is returned if the

[doesn’t correspond to an](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)

`Error`[. This might happen, for example, when the error was produced because a cycle was found in the directory tree while following symbolic links.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/struct.Error.html)

`io::Error`This method returns a borrowed value that is bound to the lifetime of the [ Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html). To
obtain an owned value, the

[can be used instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html#method.into_io_error)

`into_io_error`This is the original

[and is](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/struct.Error.html)`io::Error`notthe same as[which contains additional context about the error.](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html#impl-From%3CError%3E)`impl From<Error> for std::io::Error`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::io;
use std::path::Path;
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo") {
    match entry {
        Ok(entry) => println!("{}", entry.path().display()),
        Err(err) => {
            let path = err.path().unwrap_or(Path::new("")).display();
            println!("failed to access entry {}", path);
            if let Some(inner) = err.io_error() {
                match inner.kind() {
                    io::ErrorKind::InvalidData => {
                        println!(
                            "entry contains invalid data: {}",
                            inner)
                    }
                    io::ErrorKind::PermissionDenied => {
                        println!(
                            "Missing permission to read entry: {}",
                            inner)
                    }
                    _ => {
                        println!(
                            "Unexpected error occurred: {}",
                            inner)
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

# IntoIter in walkdir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/walkdir/latest/target-redirect/walkdir/struct.IntoIter.html

`pub struct IntoIter { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An iterator for recursively descending into a directory.

A value with this type must be constructed with the [ WalkDir](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html) type, which
uses a builder pattern to set options such as min/max depth, max open file
descriptors and whether the iterator should follow symbolic links. After
constructing a

`WalkDir`, call [at the end of the chain.](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#into_iter.v)

`.into_iter()`The order of elements yielded by this iterator is unspecified.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#781-785)#### pub fn [skip_current_dir](https://docs.rs#method.skip_current_dir)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#781-785)

#### pub fn [skip_current_dir](https://docs.rs#method.skip_current_dir)(&mut self)

Skips the current directory.

This causes the iterator to stop traversing the contents of the least recently yielded directory. This means any remaining entries in that directory will be skipped (including sub-directories).

Note that the ergonomics of this method are questionable since it borrows the iterator mutably. Namely, you must write out the looping condition manually. For example, to skip hidden entries efficiently on unix systems:

```
use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
    entry.file_name()
         .to_str()
         .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
         .unwrap_or(false)
}
let mut it = WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter();
loop {
    let entry = match it.next() {
        None => break,
        Some(Err(err)) => panic!("ERROR: {}", err),
        Some(Ok(entry)) => entry,
    };
    if is_hidden(&entry) {
        if entry.file_type().is_dir() {
            it.skip_current_dir();
        }
        continue;
    }
    println!("{}", entry.path().display());
}
```
You may find it more convenient to use the [ filter_entry](https://docs.rs#method.filter_entry) iterator
adapter. (See its documentation for the same example functionality as
above.)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#833-838)#### pub fn [filter_entry](https://docs.rs#method.filter_entry)<P>(self, predicate: P) -> [FilterEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterEntry.html)<Self, P>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#833-838)

#### pub fn [filter_entry](https://docs.rs#method.filter_entry)<P>(self, predicate: P) -> [FilterEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterEntry.html)<Self, P>

Yields only entries which satisfy the given predicate and skips descending into directories that do not satisfy the given predicate.

The predicate is applied to all entries. If the predicate is true, iteration carries on as normal. If the predicate is false, the entry is ignored and if it is a directory, it is not descended into.

This is often more convenient to use than [ skip_current_dir](https://docs.rs#method.skip_current_dir). For
example, to skip hidden files and directories efficiently on unix
systems:

```
use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
    entry.file_name()
         .to_str()
         .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
         .unwrap_or(false)
}
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo")
                     .into_iter()
                     .filter_entry(|e| !is_hidden(e)) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
Note that the iterator will still yield errors for reading entries that may not satisfy the predicate.

Note that entries skipped with [ min_depth](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.min_depth) and

[are not passed to this predicate.](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.max_depth)

`max_depth`Note that if the iterator has `contents_first` enabled, then this
method is no different than calling the standard `Iterator::filter`
method (because directory entries are yielded after they’ve been
descended into).

# FilterEntry in walkdir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/walkdir/latest/target-redirect/walkdir/struct.FilterEntry.html

`pub struct FilterEntry<I, P> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A recursive directory iterator that skips entries.

Values of this type are created by calling [ .filter_entry()](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html#method.filter_entry) on an

`IntoIter`, which is formed by calling [on a](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#into_iter.v)

`.into_iter()``WalkDir`.Directories that fail the predicate `P` are skipped. Namely, they are
never yielded and never descended into.

Entries that are skipped with the [ min_depth](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.min_depth) and

[options are not passed through this filter.](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.max_depth)

`max_depth`If opening a handle to a directory resulted in an error, then it is yielded and no corresponding call to the predicate is made.

Type parameter `I` refers to the underlying iterator and `P` refers to the
predicate, which is usually `FnMut(&DirEntry) -> bool`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

### impl<P> [FilterEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterEntry.html)<[IntoIter](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html), P>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#1144-1146)#### pub fn [filter_entry](https://docs.rs#method.filter_entry)(self, predicate: P) -> [FilterEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterEntry.html)<Self, P>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#1144-1146)

#### pub fn [filter_entry](https://docs.rs#method.filter_entry)(self, predicate: P) -> [FilterEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterEntry.html)<Self, P>

Yields only entries which satisfy the given predicate and skips descending into directories that do not satisfy the given predicate.

The predicate is applied to all entries. If the predicate is true, iteration carries on as normal. If the predicate is false, the entry is ignored and if it is a directory, it is not descended into.

This is often more convenient to use than [ skip_current_dir](https://docs.rs#method.skip_current_dir). For
example, to skip hidden files and directories efficiently on unix
systems:

```
use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
    entry.file_name()
         .to_str()
         .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
         .unwrap_or(false)
}
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo")
                     .into_iter()
                     .filter_entry(|e| !is_hidden(e)) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
Note that the iterator will still yield errors for reading entries that may not satisfy the predicate.

Note that entries skipped with [ min_depth](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.min_depth) and

[are not passed to this predicate.](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.max_depth)

`max_depth`Note that if the iterator has `contents_first` enabled, then this
method is no different than calling the standard `Iterator::filter`
method (because directory entries are yielded after they’ve been
descended into).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#1191-1193)#### pub fn [skip_current_dir](https://docs.rs#method.skip_current_dir)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/walkdir/lib.rs.html#1191-1193)

#### pub fn [skip_current_dir](https://docs.rs#method.skip_current_dir)(&mut self)

Skips the current directory.

This causes the iterator to stop traversing the contents of the least recently yielded directory. This means any remaining entries in that directory will be skipped (including sub-directories).

Note that the ergonomics of this method are questionable since it borrows the iterator mutably. Namely, you must write out the looping condition manually. For example, to skip hidden entries efficiently on unix systems:

```
use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
    entry.file_name()
         .to_str()
         .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
         .unwrap_or(false)
}
let mut it = WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter();
loop {
    let entry = match it.next() {
        None => break,
        Some(Err(err)) => panic!("ERROR: {}", err),
        Some(Ok(entry)) => entry,
    };
    if is_hidden(&entry) {
        if entry.file_type().is_dir() {
            it.skip_current_dir();
        }
        continue;
    }
    println!("{}", entry.path().display());
}
```
You may find it more convenient to use the [ filter_entry](https://docs.rs#method.filter_entry) iterator
adapter. (See its documentation for the same example functionality as
above.)

# Result in walkdir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/walkdir/latest/target-redirect/walkdir/type.Result.html

## Expand description

A result type for walkdir operations.

Note that this result type embeds the error type in this crate. This
is only useful if you care about the additional information provided by
the error (such as the path associated with the error or whether a loop
was dectected). If you want things to Just Work, then you can use
[ io::Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/type.Result.html) instead since the error type in this package will
automatically convert to an

[when using the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/type.Result.html)

`io::Result`[macro.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.try.html)

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`

- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap::Command

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

CLI Helpers
